properties.short_description: Japan's most celebrated postwar singer and actress, the 'Queen of Showa'; her enka and kayōkyoku hits such as 'Kawa no Nagare no Yō ni' and 'Yawara' defined an era.
Singer and actress who rose to fame with 'Tennessee Waltz' in 1952 and formed the beloved 'Sannin Musume' trio with Hibari Misora and Izumi Yukimura.
Jazz-influenced pop singer and actress; the third of the 'Sannin Musume' alongside Hibari Misora and Chiemi Eri.
Enka pioneer whose 'Otomi-san' (1954) and 'Wakare no Ipponsugi' became national sing-alongs.
Enka and min'yō singer with a soaring voice; 'Onna Sendō Uta' and 'Kojō' sold millions in the late 1950s.
Baritone crooner of 'mood kayō' whose 'Yūrakuchō de Aimashō' (1957) evoked Tokyo nightlife.
Singer of 'Ue o Muite Arukō' (1961), known abroad as 'Sukiyaki', the first Japanese song to top the US charts.
Film star and singer, Japan's 'eternal superstar', whose husky ballads and Nikkatsu action films defined 1960s cool.
Twin-sister vocal duo Emi and Yumi Ito, active 1959 to 1975; 'Koi no Vacance' (1963) and the Mothra song, hosts of 'Shabondama Holiday'.
Enka giant of 'Namida Bune' and 'Matsuri', a fixture of NHK's Kōhaku for five decades.
Enka singer whose 'Anko Tsubaki wa Koi no Hana' (1964) made her a star at 16; her growling 'unari' is unmistakable.
Husky-voiced enka singer of 'Erimo Misaki' (1974) and 'Ofukuro-san'.
Enka queen of 'Funauta' (1979) and 'Ame no Bojō' (1980), beloved for her smoky voice.
Teenage enka sensation of 1970 with 'Keiko no Yume wa Yoru Hiraku'.
Idol singer and actress who dominated the late 1970s before retiring at 21 in 1980.
Taiwanese singer whose Japanese-language ballads such as 'Tsugunai' and 'Toki no Nagare ni Mi o Makase' won Japan's heart.
'Yokohama Tasogare' (1971) launched one of enka's longest careers.
Idol trio of 'Haru Ichiban' (1976), whose 1978 farewell concert drew 55,000 fans.

properties.description: The first of the 48-film Tora-san series: a wandering peddler returns to Shibamata and falls hopelessly in love. Japan's most beloved comedy franchise.
Akira Kurosawa's humane epic about a gruff doctor (Toshiro Mifune) and his young intern at a clinic for the poor in Edo.
Kon Ichikawa's lyrical documentary of the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, seen by millions in cinemas across Japan.
Masaki Kobayashi's painterly anthology of four ghost stories from Lafcadio Hearn.
Yoji Yamada's road movie across Hokkaido: an ex-convict (Ken Takakura) hopes his wife (Chieko Baisho) has hung a yellow handkerchief to welcome him home.

akas.value: 幸福の黄色いハンカチ

properties.description: Yoshitaro Nomura's sweeping mystery from Seicho Matsumoto's novel, with a famous piano-concerto finale.
Kurosawa's first color film: vivid vignettes of life in a Tokyo shantytown.
Kurosawa's Palme d'Or-winning epic of a thief who must impersonate a dead warlord.
Kei Kumai's drama about a woman sent to Borneo as a 'karayuki-san'; Kinuyo Tanaka won the Berlin Silver Bear.

akas.value: サンダカン八番娼館 望郷

properties.description: Kenji Mizoguchi's portrait of a telephone operator in Osaka trapped between family duty and her boss.
A 13-year-old Hibari Misora stars as a street singer in postwar Tokyo, singing the title song that became her signature.
Ishirō Honda's original monster film, a somber allegory of the atomic age.
Kurosawa's masterpiece: a village hires seven masterless samurai to defend its harvest.
Ken Takakura's breakout 'ninkyo' yakuza film, launching a nine-film series that filled cinemas through the late 1960s.
Toho's blockbuster disaster film from Sakyo Komatsu's bestseller, the talk of New Year 1974.
NHK's New Year's Eve singing contest between red and white teams; Hibari Misora headlined it many times.
The Drifters' live Saturday-night variety show, with slapstick skits watched by half the country.
Long-running jidaigeki in which a retired vice-shogun travels Japan in disguise, righting wrongs with his crest at the climax of every episode.
Tsuburaya's giant hero fought a new monster every week in 1966-67.
Sunday-evening variety show hosted by The Peanuts with Hana Hajime and the Crazy Cats.
NHK morning drama following a woman's life from Meiji-era poverty to supermarket success; its 52.6% rating is still a record.
Police drama led by Yujiro Ishihara as 'Boss', famous for its young detectives' nicknames and dramatic deaths.
Osaka's comedy troupe broadcast every Saturday lunchtime from Namba, with running gags every Kansai household knows.
Okonomiyaki restaurant on Dotonbori since 1945, known for its grated-yam 'yamaimo-yaki'.
Crab restaurant whose giant moving crab sign has loomed over Dotonbori since 1962.

akas.value: かに道楽 道頓堀本店

properties.description: Deep-fried skewers in Shinsekai since 1929, with the famous 'no double dipping' sauce rule.

akas.value: 串かつだるま 新世界総本店

properties.description: Curry-rice house founded in 1910, famous for its 'meibutsu curry' with a raw egg on top, a favorite of novelist Sakunosuke Oda.
Birthplace of omurice (1925), served on tatami in an old townhouse off Shinsaibashi.

akas.value: 北極星 心斎橋本店

properties.description: The takoyaki originator, founded in 1933 in Tamade; small dashi-flavored balls served without sauce.
Sukiyaki restaurant and butcher on Dotonbori since 1919, with a Western-style grill next door.

akas.value: はり重 道頓堀本店

properties.description: Pressed 'hako-zushi' specialist in Awaji-machi, founded in 1841.
Osaka's sweet-then-fiery curry counter, founded in 1947 and still queued for at lunchtime.
Shinsekai's tower, rebuilt in 1956, with the Billiken good-luck statue on the observation deck.
Canal-side entertainment district of neon and street food, watched over by the Glico running man since 1935.
Hideyoshi's castle, its main tower rebuilt in 1931, set in a park of plum and cherry trees.
Ivy-covered 1924 ballpark, home of the Hanshin Tigers and the national high-school baseball tournaments.
Stone-paved alley of tiny restaurants beside Hozenji temple, where visitors splash water on the moss-covered Fudō statue.
Osaka's first public park (1891), a river island with a rose garden and the red-brick Central Public Hall.
Retro 'New World' district laid out in 1912, all kushikatsu shops, shogi parlors and the Tsutenkaku tower.
City zoo opened in 1915, a classic family outing beside Tennoji Park.
Neo-Renaissance theater on Dotonbori, opened in 1923, long a stage for stars of song and kabuki.
Taro Okamoto's 70-metre sculpture, the symbol of Expo '70, still standing in the Expo Commemorative Park in Suita.
One of Japan's oldest shrines, with its arched red Sorihashi bridge and huge New Year crowds.
Japan's first railway-terminal department store (1929), with the dining hall that generations of Osaka families visited on special days.
The former imperial capital, under an hour from Osaka: temples, geisha lanes and autumn maples.
Deer park and the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji; the classic school-trip day out from Osaka.
Bamboo grove, the Togetsukyō bridge and river boats in western Kyoto.
One of Japan's oldest hot-spring towns, in the hills behind Kobe, with iron-red 'golden' baths.
White-sand beach and seaside hot springs on the Wakayama coast, a honeymoon favorite of the 1960s and 70s.
Japan's largest lake, a short train ride northeast of Osaka, with beaches, boat cruises and the 'Biwako Shūkō no Uta' song everyone knows.
Mountaintop monastery town of Shingon Buddhism in Wakayama, reached by cable car.
Home of Ise Grand Shrine, Japan's most sacred Shinto site, and the once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage of the Showa years.
Island across the Akashi Strait from Kobe, known for onions, the Naruto whirlpools and quiet beaches.
Hot-spring capital of Kyushu, famous for its steaming 'hells' and sand baths.
Seaside hot-spring resort near Tokyo, the honeymoon and company-trip town of the Showa era.
